topline.text: Today's the big one: Chancellor John Healey delivers his first Budget this afternoon, with the OBR's updated Economic and Fiscal Outlook published alongside it.

Healey has declined to rule tax rises in or out; economists think the fiscal headroom his predecessor built up has likely narrowed, so treat any school-funding figures doing the rounds today as speculation until the statement itself.
Otherwise a genuinely quiet day - Sheffield schools stay closed for half term until Monday 2 November, and no major new UK schools story broke in the last 24 hours.
Reminder: the NEU's formal strike ballot over pay, funding and workload is still open and closes 15 December - turnout in the earlier indicative vote was under 50%.

diary.text: Sheffield schools' autumn half term continues.
Today: Chancellor John Healey's first Budget, with the OBR's Economic and Fiscal Outlook published alongside it.
NEU's formal strike ballot over pay, funding and workload closes.
UK City of Culture 2029 winner announced; Sheffield is one of four finalists.

items.lede: All eyes on this afternoon's Budget.
items.body: Chancellor John Healey - who took the role in July when Andy Burnham became Prime Minister - delivers his first Budget today, with the Office for Budget Responsibility's forecast published alongside it. He has so far declined to confirm or rule out tax rises, and analysts think the fiscal headroom built up by his predecessor has likely shrunk on weaker growth and higher borrowing costs. Nothing is confirmed yet on mainstream or high-needs school funding.
items.action: Hold off on budget-planning assumptions until this afternoon's statement and the DfE's response to it.

items.body: The NEU's formal strike ballot over pay, funding and workload - covering teachers and support staff separately - remains open and closes 15 December. In the earlier indicative ballot, 96% of responding teachers backed rejecting the pay offer and said they'd be prepared to take action, though turnout was under 50%.

box.label: Jargon-buster - fiscal headroom
box.intro: Today's Budget speculation keeps coming back to this phrase.
box.text: "Fiscal headroom" is the gap between what the Chancellor plans to spend or borrow and the limit set by the government's own fiscal rules, as judged by OBR forecasts. Less headroom this time around means less room for new spending promises - schools included - without tax rises or cuts elsewhere.
